files.text:
scroll

In the summer of 1863, ill and kept to the house, Darwin set pots of climbing plants on the sill of his study window and watched them by the hour. The tip of a young passionflower is never still: it sweeps a slow ellipse, about once an hour, feeling for something to hold. The tendrils revolve as well, held out straight and stiff, and when one touches a stick it bends within half a minute and is soon wound fast. Then the free length coils into a spring that draws the stem in, turning one way for half its length and back the other way for the rest, because both its ends are held. The Spanish friars who first saw the flower read the Passion in it: the crown of thorns in the corona, three nails in the styles, five wounds in the anthers, and ten faithful apostles in its petals and sepals.

# pretext-vine A passionflower climbs a paragraph, and the paragraph makes room for it. The text is set by Cheng Lou's pretext. As you scroll, a shoot comes up out of the lower margin and climbs through the type, its tip sweeping slow ellipses; wherever the stem crosses a line, pretext re-sets that line as two runs, one each side of the stem, each justified on its own, and the words ease aside as the tip comes up to them. At the nodes, palmate leaves cut from Curtis's 1787 plate of *Passiflora caerulea* unfold from folded halves, and tendrils revolve while the stem climbs, then one after another catch real ascenders (an l, h, k, d, b or f) and coil round them, the letter painted in front of the turns that pass behind it, and wind their free length into a spring that reverses its hand halfway along. At the top the painted bud from the same plate swells, the paragraph's corner flows aside, and the bud opens into Redouté's flower: its tepals spread, its corona fans out, its stamens and styles rise, and the open flower is the plate's own pixels, the only colour on the page. Scroll back and it ungrows and the words flow back. ```html

In the summer of 1863, ill and kept to the house, Darwin…

``` Or `import { pretextVine } from './pretext-vine.js'` and call `pretextVine(section, { seed, side })`. It returns `destroy()`, which also carries `growTo(progress)`: `destroy.growTo(0.4)` drives the growth yourself (0 to 1), `destroy.growTo(null)` hands it back to the scroll. The same handle is on the element as `section.pretextVine`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|---------|--------------| | `data-seed` | `seed` | `7` | Every choice (the sway of the climb, leaf angles and sizes, which letters the tendrils take, the hand of each coil) comes from this seed. Same seed, same plant, at any scroll position. | | `data-side` | `side` | `left` | `left` or `right`: the top corner of the paragraph where the flower opens. The vine starts low on the other side and leans across to it. | The paragraph's own CSS (`.pv-text` font family, weight and colour) sets the type; the size is chosen by the script: about 26px on a wide desktop down to 16-17px on a phone, shrunk if the text, the flower and the stem's way in would not fit the stage. ## How it works 1. **The plant first.** The stem's path is planned before any text is set: it enters in the far margin and leans across the paragraph toward the flower's corner with a seeded sway, at most ~4.5em sideways per line, crossing each line either in a margin or at least 5em inside the column (so the runs either side can hold words). Between lines it is a cubic S, upright where it crosses a line and leaning across the leading. 2. **Text flows round it** (the Cheng Lou part). Each crossing is an obstacle on its line: the stem alone, plus about 0.35em of air each side (leaves and tendrils never displace text; they lie under it with the paper halo). The paragraph, hyphenated with TeX's patterns (Liang's algorithm, Knuth's US English patterns in `vendor/hyphen`, the same as page-turn), is flowed with pretext (`prepareWithSegments`, `layoutNextLineRange`, `materializeLineRange`) into the runs each line has left, each run justified on its own. A run narrower than about three words is not set: the stem simply passes between the words there, behind the type. If a run beside the stem would still be left ragged by more than about an em, the line is set whole instead and the stem passes behind it. The flower is an obstacle too: a star through its ten petal tips, over the paragraph's top corner. One layout is computed per obstacle, in the order the vine reaches it (stem crossings bottom to top, then the flower in four steps), and scroll position picks a point between two of them. The units placed are syllables, so a word can break at a hyphen in one layout and not the next: syllables that stay on their line slide; ones that change line fade out first and in last, so nothing passes through anything else. 3. **Growth** is a function of progress only. Progress maps to `tau`, a length of growth; the stem is drawn to `min(tau, length)` and every node's age is `tau` minus its place. The stem is up by ~55% of the runway; the bud swells and the corner clears from 55% to 75%; the tendrils take hold one after another from 68% to 76% and coil by ~84%; the flower opens from 75% to 95%; then it holds. 4. **Circumnutation.** The last ~1.7 lines of stem are pushed off the path by an ellipse (0.9em across, 0.35em along) whose phase is `tau`: one sweep per ~5 lines of growth. Older stem has settled where the path lies. 5. **The stem** is drawn as the plate engraves it: a tapered body from a woody olive foot to a green tip, a dark line down its shadow side with fine hatching across it, and a light line down the lit side. 6. **Leaves.** A leaf at every other node, and at the nodes between where one sits in the clear, plus two young folded leaves on the shoot above the flower. Each is placed by trying petiole angles and sizes against the final layout: text under it (never more than about a word), off the stage, over the flower or another leaf. Each lobe is a real painted lobe from Curtis's plate drawn down its own axis; young leaves hold their lobes together and folded. Leaves lie under the type, and a hairline paper halo round every glyph keeps a word over a leaf readable. 7. **Tendrils.** One with each leaf, from the axil. It revolves straight and stiff with a hooked tip while the stem climbs, then (once the words have stopped moving, so the letter it takes will stay where it is) its sweep closes onto an ascender a few ems away, it wraps the letter's stem 2.5 turns (1.8 on a phone), and its free length coils into a helix whose phase runs forward to the middle and back again (a perversion: one hand, a short straight, the other hand), the projected loops leaning one way then the other, and the node is drawn a few px toward the letter. A tendril with nothing in reach coils on itself into a loose one-handed spiral. Tendril runs behind a letter go on the back canvas, runs in front on the front one. 8. **The flower.** The bud is Curtis's painted bud on its stalk, muted like the leaves; it swells, then foreshortens as it turns to face you and gives way to Redouté's frontal flower, cut from the plate into three layers that share one frame: the ten tepals (with the corona and stamens painted out beneath them), the corona (rings and filament bars), and the stamens and styles. The tepals open as wedges of the plate, each scaled along its own axis by the sine of its opening angle (sepals first, petals after); the corona fans out from tight and turned; the stamens and styles rise last; and over the last few percent the layers give way to the uncut plate, so the open flower is the plate's own pixels. ## The real thing What a real observer sees (Darwin, *The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants*, 1875; Goriely & Tabor, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 1998), and what was kept: - **Circumnutation:** the young internodes of *Passiflora gracilis* revolve faster than any plant Darwin timed, about an hour a turn, sweeping wide ellipses. Kept: the elliptical sweep at the growing end, decaying down the stem. Compressed: one sweep per ~5 lines of growth. - **Tendrils:** straight and revolving while they search; a touched tip bends within 25-30 seconds and soon winds round the support; then the free part coils into a spring and shortens, drawing the stem in. Because both ends are held, it cannot gain twist: it coils one way along part of its length and the other way along the rest, with a short straight between. Kept, including the reversal and the pull on the node. Simplified: always exactly one perversion, at the middle. - **Leaves:** *P. caerulea* is palmately five-lobed, alternate, one leaf per node with a tendril (and a flower bud) in the axil, glands on the petiole. Young leaves come folded and spread. Kept, except that only the top node carries a flower. - **Flower:** a long ovoid bud between leafy bracts, sepals horned; ten perianth parts open flat; the corona of filaments banded purple, white and blue; five stamens hanging their anthers; three styles with capitate stigmas. Kept, in the plate's own painting. The real opening takes about an hour on a summer morning; here it takes a fifth of the scroll. Simplified: the opening is the frontal view only (tepals lengthen from pointing at you to lying flat), and the bud is a different plate's than the flower. - **Timing:** in life a tendril catches whatever it meets while the shoot grows; here they all wait, revolving, until the words have settled, then catch hold bottom to top, so a letter never moves out of a coil. ## Tuning - **Pacing:** `tauOf` (stem), `openOf` (flower), the flower ramps in `layout` (`p0`, `p1`: when the corner clears) and the contact schedule (`pc`, 0.68 to 0.76). `--pv-runway` (default `280svh`) sets how long all of it takes. - **The climb:** the step limit (4.5em per line), the sway (0.13 of the column), the inside margin (5em) and the stem's clearance (`clear`: half the stem plus 0.35em each side). - **The flow:** `minRun` (5.5em, about three words: the narrowest run worth setting), the justification limit (2.6 spaces) and the hole limit (0.9em of rag beside the stem, beyond which the line is set whole). - **Leaves:** `leafS` (2.5em desktop, 2.25em phone, the middle lobe's length, varied 0.72-1.12 by seed) and `wordArea` (how much text a leaf may cover). - **Flower:** `Rf` (5.2em on desktop, 90-140px; up to 100px on a phone) and `E` (its centre; desktop just outside the column's top corner, phone above the first line). The opening's stages are the `smooth()` windows in `drawFlower`. - **The flower assets** are cut by a script (Python, scipy) in the build notes: the plate is masked against its paper, the filament bars found by colour and radial shape, the stamens and styles by colour inside a drawn outline, and what each layer hides is filled by normalised convolution. `FL` holds the frame (centre, and the ten tip angles and lengths); `BUD` the bud's stalk end and tip. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|----------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the stage, and the hairline halo round the letters (read from the section's background) | | `--ink` | `#141312` | the words (the spans copy `.pv-text`'s colour) | | `--pv-serif` | `var(--serif)` | the face; the demo uses EB Garamond for its tall ascenders | | `--pv-runway` | `280svh` | length of the scroll runway | Vine colours (stem, tendril) are in `C` at the top of the drawing section; the flower's palette is inline in `drawFlower`, matched to the plate. ## Accessibility and motion - The real `

` stays in the DOM, visually hidden once the vine is live: it is what screen readers read. The positioned word spans are `aria-hidden` but are real text, so they can be selected and found. Without JS, or if pretext or the atlas fails to load, the paragraph is a plain paragraph. - Reduced motion: no runway; the finished vine with the flower open. - Phone: the paragraph reflows at 390px (about 18 lines at 16-17px) round the stem and the flower, which opens over the first line's corner; every other node carries a leaf. The stage has `touch-action: pan-y`; nothing traps scrolling. - Cost: two canvases the size of the stage (DPR up to 2, or 3 on a phone narrower than 620px, where the stage is small and the 1px tendrils and filaments need it). A frame redraws stem, leaves, tendrils and flower (well under a few ms) and only runs while the shown growth is catching up with the scroll; at rest, off screen or in a hidden tab, nothing runs. `destroy()` removes canvases, spans, listeners and observers. ## Events For sound later (bubbling `CustomEvent`s on the section; none fire for the state the page opens on): - `pretext-vine:touch` — a tendril meets its letter (`detail.letter`). - `pretext-vine:bloom` — the flower opens past halfway. ## Credits - [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) by Cheng Lou, MIT (`vendor/pretext`, unmodified, see its `LICENSE` and `VERSION`). - Hyphenation patterns: Knuth's `hyphen.tex` US English patterns as converted for LibreOffice (`vendor/hyphen`, see its `LICENSE` and `VERSION`). - Leaf lobes and the bud cut from *Passiflora caerulea*, The Botanical Magazine plate 28 (1787), drawn by Sydenham Edwards for William Curtis, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. - The flower cut from *Passiflora coerulea / Grenadille bleue*, Traité des arbres et arbustes (Nouveau Duhamel), t. 2 no. 12, painted by Pierre-Joseph Redouté and engraved by Mixelle, public domain (New York Public Library), via Wikimedia Commons. See `assets/credits.json`. - Behaviour after Charles Darwin, *The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants* (1875), and A. Goriely and M. Tabor, "Spontaneous helix hand reversal and tendril perversion in climbing plants", *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80 (1998).

version 2010-03-16

Changes

- forbid hyphenation at 1-character distances from dashes (eg. ad=d-on)
  and at the dashes (fix for OpenOffice.org 3.2)
- set correct LEFTHYPHENMIN = 2, RIGHTHYPHENMIN = 3
- handle apostrophes (forbid *o'=clock etc.)
- set COMPOUNDLEFTHYPHENMIN, COMPOUNDRIGHTHYPHENMIN values
- UTF-8 encoding
- Unicode ligature support
